cards.front: A change to DNA's chemical structure that is not yet a heritable sequence change is called a {{c1::lesion}}.
cards.quote: A lesion is a change to DNA's chemical structure, not yet a mutation, a heritable sequence change.
cards.section: Damage is constant: the lesions

cards.front: How does a DNA lesion usually become a mutation?
cards.back: Replication converts it into a normal-looking base pair on both strands, so the change becomes heritable.
cards.quote: A lesion usually becomes one when replication converts it into a normal-looking base pair on both strands.
cards.section: Damage is constant: the lesions

cards.front: A cytosine in DNA is deaminated to uracil and never repaired. What can the DNA look like after two rounds of replication?
cards.back: A·T can sit where G·C had been: the first round puts A opposite U, the next can leave A·T.
cards.quote: If it remains, one round of replication puts A opposite U; the next can leave A·T where G·C had been.
cards.section: Damage is constant: the lesions

cards.front: What two kinds of lesion does ultraviolet light make in DNA, and where does each form?
cards.back: A cyclobutane pyrimidine dimer or a 6-4 photoproduct, each joining two neighboring pyrimidines on the same strand.
cards.quote: UV joins two neighboring pyrimidines on the same strand into a cyclobutane pyrimidine dimer or a 6-4 photoproduct.
cards.section: Damage is constant: the lesions

cards.front: Which base does 8-oxoguanine tend to pair with, and which does O6-methylguanine pair with?
cards.back: 8-oxoguanine can pair with adenine; O6-methylguanine pairs with thymine.
cards.quote: Reactive oxygen produces 8-oxoguanine, which can pair with adenine. Alkylating agents add methyl groups; O6-methylguanine pairs with thymine.
cards.section: Damage is constant: the lesions

cards.front: What does photolyase do, and why can human skin not use this route for UV dimers?
cards.back: It uses blue and near-UV light to split pyrimidine dimers into separate bases. Humans lack the photolyases that reverse UV dimers.
cards.quote: They work in bacteria, yeast and plants, but humans lack the photolyases that reverse UV dimers, so your skin cannot use this route.
cards.section: Reversing and cutting out: direct reversal, BER and NER

cards.front: Why is O6-methylguanine methyltransferase (MGMT) called a suicide enzyme?
cards.back: It moves the methyl group onto a cysteine in its own active site. That restores the base but inactivates the protein, so one molecule repairs one lesion.
cards.quote: One molecule repairs one lesion, so it is called a suicide enzyme.
cards.section: Reversing and cutting out: direct reversal, BER and NER

cards.front: In base excision repair, what does the DNA glycosylase do, and what is left behind?
cards.back: It flips out the damaged base and cuts its bond to the sugar, leaving an AP site (a sugar with no base).
cards.quote: Each DNA glycosylase recognizes one damaged base or a few related ones, flips it out and cuts its bond to the sugar, leaving an AP site.
cards.section: Reversing and cutting out: direct reversal, BER and NER

cards.front: Why can one nucleotide excision repair pathway fix many different lesions?
cards.back: It recognizes helix distortion rather than one particular chemical group.
cards.quote: Because it recognizes distortion rather than one chemical group, one pathway handles many lesions.
cards.section: Reversing and cutting out: direct reversal, BER and NER

cards.front: A cell has working uracil-DNA glycosylase but no working AP endonuclease. After cytosine deamination, which intermediate should accumulate: uracil in DNA, AP sites with an intact backbone, or sealed repaired DNA?
cards.back: AP sites with an intact backbone. Glycosylase removes the uracil, but the next cut, by AP endonuclease, cannot happen. Some glycosylases also cut the backbone, so this does not fit every BER substrate.
cards.quote: Glycosylase removes uracil, but AP endonuclease cannot make the next cut.
cards.section: Reversing and cutting out: direct reversal, BER and NER

cards.front: In human nucleotide excision repair, which nucleases make the 5′ cut and the 3′ cut, and which complex opens the DNA?
cards.back: XPF-ERCC1 cuts 5′ and XPG cuts 3′. TFIIH, with helicase activity, opens the DNA and helps verify the lesion.
cards.quote: XPF-ERCC1 makes the 5′ cut and XPG the 3′ cut.
cards.section: Reversing and cutting out: direct reversal, BER and NER

cards.front: A lesion barely distorts the helix but strongly stalls RNA polymerase in an active gene. Which recognition route gives nucleotide excision repair its clearest starting signal?
cards.back: The transcription-coupled route: the stalled polymerase supplies the signal. Both routes then feed the same opening, cutting and refill steps.
cards.quote: In a transcribed gene, RNA polymerase stalled at a lesion flags the damage.
cards.section: Reversing and cutting out: direct reversal, BER and NER

cards.front: A drug forms bulky adducts on guanines in a human cell. Which repair pathway should mainly remove them, and why not base excision repair?
cards.back: Nucleotide excision repair. The adducts are bulky and helix-distorting, which NER handles; BER handles small, non-bulky base lesions.
cards.quote: Nucleotide excision repair (NER) handles bulky, helix-distorting lesions: UV dimers, 6-4 photoproducts and adducts from drugs such as cisplatin.
cards.section: Reversing and cutting out: direct reversal, BER and NER

cards.front: In E. coli, why is the new strand briefly distinguishable from the template, and what is the state of the DNA called?
cards.back: Dam methylation of GATC adenines lags behind the fork, so only the template is methylated: hemimethylated DNA.
cards.quote: Dam methylase methylates adenine in GATC sequences only after the fork has passed
cards.section: Fixing the copier's mistakes: mismatch repair

cards.front: In E. coli mismatch repair, what do MutS, MutL and MutH each do?
cards.back: MutS binds the mismatch; MutL joins it; together they activate MutH, which nicks the unmethylated strand at GATC.
cards.quote: MutS binds the mismatch, MutL joins it and they activate MutH, which nicks the unmethylated strand at GATC.
cards.section: Fixing the copier's mistakes: mismatch repair

cards.front: Eukaryotes have no MutH. What do they appear to use to tell the new strand from the template?
cards.back: Strand breaks: new DNA has free ends, at the growing tip and between Okazaki fragments.
cards.quote: They appear to read strand breaks instead: new DNA has free ends, at the tip of the growing strand and between Okazaki fragments.
cards.section: Fixing the copier's mistakes: mismatch repair

cards.front: Purified E. coli mismatch-repair proteins act on circular DNA with one G·T mismatch and a GATC site 1 kilobase away. If only the T strand is methylated, the G is replaced by A. If only the G strand is methylated, the T is replaced by C. If both are methylated, little repair occurs. What do these results show?
cards.back: The unmethylated strand is excised and replaced. The system uses methylation as the strand signal, and the GATC site can direct repair from a distance of about 1 kilobase.
cards.why: Rests on the rule that mismatch repair needs strand identity.
cards.quote: In Paul Modrich's purified system, a GATC site about 1 kilobase away still directed repair.
cards.section: Fixing the copier's mistakes: mismatch repair

cards.front: In the lesson's model, a polymerase errs once per 10^5 nucleotides, proofreading removes 99% of errors and mismatch repair removes 99.9% of the rest. How many errors remain per daughter genome of 6.4 x 10^9 bp?
cards.back: Surviving fractions are 10^-2 and 10^-3, so the rate is 10^-5 x 10^-2 x 10^-3 = 10^-10 per bp. 6.4 x 10^9 x 10^-10 = 0.64 errors per daughter genome.
cards.quote: Multiply the stages, because each acts on what the last one missed.
cards.section: Fixing the copier's mistakes: mismatch repair

cards.front: Same model (error 10^-5 per nucleotide, mismatch repair removes 99.9%, 6.4 x 10^9 bp per daughter genome), but proofreading is lost and mismatch repair still works. About how many errors per daughter genome?
cards.back: Rate is 10^-5 x 10^-3 = 10^-8 per bp. 6.4 x 10^9 x 10^-8 = 64 errors per daughter genome.
cards.quote: Count errors per daughter genome: each daughter cell inherits a diploid genome of about 6.4 x 10^9 base pairs, one strand of each pair newly made.
cards.section: Fixing the copier's mistakes: mismatch repair

cards.front: Same model, but mismatch repair is removed and proofreading (99%) still works. What is the error rate per bp, the errors per daughter genome, and the fold change from the intact model?
cards.back: Rate is 10^-5 x 10^-2 = 10^-7 per bp; 6.4 x 10^9 x 10^-7 = 640 errors per daughter genome. Versus 0.64, that is a thousandfold rise.
cards.quote: So with these numbers, losing mismatch repair raises the error rate a thousandfold, from under one error per daughter genome to hundreds.
cards.section: Fixing the copier's mistakes: mismatch repair

cards.front: Besides base-base mismatches, what else does human mismatch repair correct?
cards.back: Small loops left when the polymerase slips on a repeat.
cards.quote: Human mismatch repair also corrects small loops left when the polymerase slips on a repeat.
cards.section: Fixing the copier's mistakes: mismatch repair

cards.front: In non-homologous end joining, ring-shaped {{c1::Ku}} binds each broken end and recruits the kinase DNA-PKcs.
cards.back: XRCC4 with DNA ligase IV later joins the processed ends.
cards.quote: Ring-shaped Ku binds each end and recruits the kinase DNA-PKcs.
cards.section: Broken chromosomes: end joining and homologous recombination

cards.front: Why can non-homologous end joining change the sequence at a break, and why is calling it simply error-prone an overstatement?
cards.back: With no template, processed ends can lose or gain a few bases. But clean, compatible ends are often rejoined exactly.
cards.quote: NHEJ uses no template, so if the ends had to be processed, a few bases may be gained or lost at the joint.
cards.section: Broken chromosomes: end joining and homologous recombination

cards.front: Why does homologous recombination act mainly in S and G2 in dividing cells?
cards.back: The best template is the sister chromatid, which exists only after replication. In meiosis the homologous chromosome can serve.
cards.quote: The best template is the sister chromatid, made during replication, so HR acts mainly in S and G2; in meiosis, breaks are repaired from the homologous chromosome.
cards.section: Broken chromosomes: end joining and homologous recombination

cards.front: In homologous recombination, what does the recombinase do, and what structure results?
cards.back: RecA (E. coli) or Rad51 (eukaryotes) invades the matching duplex, making a D-loop where the 3′ end primes synthesis.
cards.quote: The recombinase (RecA in E. coli, Rad51 in eukaryotes) invades the matching duplex, making a displacement loop (D-loop) where the 3′ end primes synthesis.
cards.section: Broken chromosomes: end joining and homologous recombination

cards.front: A human cell in G1 has a double-strand break in a chromosome. Which route is it most likely to use, given what intact information remains?
cards.back: Non-homologous end joining. In G1 no sister chromatid exists, so the cell has only the two ends; HR acts mainly in S and G2.
cards.quote: a double-strand break may have only its ends unless a homologous template exists.

cards.front: What can happen to Holliday junctions before chromosomes separate, and what decides whether a crossover results?
cards.back: They are dissolved (no crossover) or cut by resolvases; a crossover forms or not depending on which strands are cut.
cards.quote: Before chromosome separation, these junctions are dissolved (no crossover) or cut by resolvases, giving a crossover or not depending on which strands are cut.
cards.section: Broken chromosomes: end joining and homologous recombination

cards.front: In the usual finish of homologous recombination, the extended strand leaves the D-loop and pairs with the other end. What is this called, and is there a crossover?
cards.back: Synthesis-dependent strand annealing (SDSA); it forms no crossover.
cards.quote: the extended strand leaves the D-loop and pairs with the other end, is synthesis-dependent strand annealing (SDSA); it forms no crossover.
cards.section: Broken chromosomes: end joining and homologous recombination

cards.front: Which repair pathway do most forms of xeroderma pigmentosum disrupt, what is the inheritance pattern, and what is the clinical consequence?
cards.back: Nucleotide excision repair; autosomal recessive. UV dimers in skin go unrepaired, associated with sunlight-induced skin cancers.
cards.quote: Most forms disrupt NER, so UV dimers in skin cells go unrepaired, and the condition is associated with sunlight-induced skin cancers.
cards.section: When repair fails: three human conditions

cards.front: What is the defect in the XP variant, whose cells have normal excision?
cards.back: A mutation in the gene for DNA polymerase eta, a bypass polymerase; cells cannot replicate efficiently past UV damage.
cards.quote: One form, the XP variant, has normal excision.
cards.section: When repair fails: three human conditions

cards.front: Compare an affected person with two nonworking XP alleles to a Lynch syndrome carrier with one working MSH2 allele. Whose normal cells should already lack the relevant repair pathway?
cards.back: The person with XP. One working MSH2 allele usually supports repair in the carrier's normal cells; losing it can remove repair in a tumor lineage.
cards.quote: One working allele is usually enough for repair, so their normal cells repair mismatches.
cards.section: When repair fails: three human conditions

cards.front: What is the inheritance pattern of Lynch syndrome, and which genes are involved?
cards.back: Dominantly inherited predisposition; germline variants in MLH1, MSH2, MSH6 or PMS2, or an EPCAM 3′ deletion silencing MSH2.
cards.quote: Lynch syndrome is a dominantly inherited predisposition to colorectal, endometrial and other cancers, with risks that vary by gene.
cards.section: When repair fails: three human conditions

cards.front: Which repair route do BRCA1 and BRCA2 support, and why are cells lacking them sensitive to PARP inhibitors?
cards.back: Homologous recombination. HR-deficient cells are unusually sensitive to PARP inhibitors, an example of synthetic lethality.
cards.quote: HR-deficient cells are unusually sensitive to PARP inhibitors, an example of synthetic lethality.
cards.section: When repair fails: three human conditions

cards.front: A reporter gives GFP-positive cells when an I-SceI break is repaired by homologous recombination: 2.4% in parental cells, 0.03% in BRCA2-mutant cells, 1.8% in BRCA2-mutant cells given working BRCA2 cDNA. What do these results show?
cards.back: BRCA2 loss cuts this repair about 80-fold (2.4 / 0.03 = 80), and the cDNA rescues it, to 75% of parental (1.8 / 2.4). BRCA2 is needed for efficient HR.
cards.why: Rests on the lesson's rule that BRCA2 is needed for efficient HR.
cards.quote: BRCA2-mutant human and mouse cell lines showed 6-fold to more than 100-fold less homology-directed repair, depending on the line.
cards.section: When repair fails: three human conditions

cards.front: A person has one germline pathogenic MSH2 variant. Extracts of normal colon cells repair a mismatched test DNA, but extracts of their colon tumor do not, and the tumor's short repeats vary in length from cell to cell. What explains the tumor?
cards.back: The tumor lost or inactivated its remaining working MSH2 allele, so it lacks mismatch repair and slippage in repeats goes uncorrected.
cards.why: Rests on: one working allele usually suffices; the tumor lineage loses the second.
cards.quote: One working MSH2 allele usually supports repair in the carrier's normal cells; losing it can remove repair in a tumor lineage.
cards.section: When repair fails: three human conditions

cards.front: Four XP fibroblast lines show low repair after UV. Fused pairs: P1+P3 low, P2+P4 low, all other pairs normal. How many complementation groups are there, and what next step identifies the genes?
cards.back: Two groups: {P1, P3} and {P2, P4}. Same-gene pairs stay low; different-gene pairs complement. Transfect each group with cloned NER candidate genes and see which restores repair, then sequence that gene in the patients.
cards.quote: P1+P3 stays low, so P1 and P3 are defective in the same gene.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Two patients' cells show reduced survival after UV. Patient A has low unscheduled DNA synthesis; patient B has normal excision but cannot replicate past UV damage. Name the defect most likely in each.
cards.back: A: a defect in a nucleotide excision repair gene (XP complementation group). B: the XP variant, a defect in bypass polymerase eta.
cards.why: Combines the NER and XP-variant sections.
cards.quote: Its cells cannot replicate efficiently past UV damage, and in 1999 two groups, Masutani and colleagues
cards.section: When repair fails: three human conditions
